title: No. 19 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton & Madison)
paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

The examples of ancient confederacies cited in my last paper have not used up the supply of experimental instruction on this subject. There are existing institutions, founded on a similar principle, that deserve particular attention. The first that comes to mind is the Germanic body.

In the early ages of Christianity, Germany was occupied by seven distinct nations, with no common chief. The Franks, one of these nations, conquered the Gauls and founded the kingdom that took its name from them. In the ninth century Charlemagne, its warlike monarch, carried his victorious arms in every direction, and Germany became part of his vast dominions. When his sons divided up the empire, this part was set up as a separate and independent realm. Charlemagne and his immediate descendants held real imperial power, along with its symbols and dignity. But the principal vassals, whose fiefs had become hereditary and who composed the national diets that Charlemagne had not abolished, gradually threw off the yoke and rose to sovereign jurisdiction and independence. The force of imperial sovereignty was not enough to restrain such powerful dependents, or to preserve the unity and tranquility of the empire. The most furious private wars, with every kind of calamity, were waged between the various princes and states. The imperial authority, unable to keep public order, declined by stages until it was almost extinct in the anarchy that filled the long interval between the death of the last Suabian emperor and the accession of the first Austrian one. In the eleventh century the emperors enjoyed full sovereignty; in the fifteenth they had little more than the symbols and decorations of power.

Out of this feudal system, which itself has many of the important features of a confederacy, has grown the federal system that makes up the Germanic empire. Its powers are vested in a diet representing the component members of the confederacy; in the emperor, who is the executive magistrate, with a veto on the diet's decrees; and in the imperial chamber and the aulic council, two judicial tribunals with supreme jurisdiction over disputes that concern the empire or arise among its members.

The diet has the general power of legislating for the empire, of making war and peace, contracting alliances, assessing quotas of troops and money, building fortresses, regulating coinage, admitting new members, and subjecting disobedient members to the ban of the empire, by which the offending party is stripped of his sovereign rights and his possessions are forfeited. Members of the confederacy are expressly forbidden to enter into compacts harmful to the empire, to impose tolls and duties on each other's trade without the consent of the emperor and diet, to alter the value of money, to do injustice to one another, or to give aid or refuge to disturbers of the public peace. The ban is pronounced against any who break these restrictions. Members of the diet, in their official capacity, are subject in all cases to be judged by the emperor and diet, and in their private capacities by the aulic council and imperial chamber.

The emperor's prerogatives are numerous. The most important are: his exclusive right to make proposals to the diet; to veto its resolutions; to name ambassadors; to confer dignities and titles; to fill vacant electorates; to found universities; to grant privileges that do not harm the states of the empire; to receive and apply the public revenues; and generally to watch over the public safety. In certain cases the electors form a council to advise him. As emperor he holds no territory within the empire and receives no revenue for his support. But his revenue and dominions in his other capacities make him one of the most powerful princes in Europe.

From such a parade of constitutional powers, in the representatives and head of this confederacy, the natural assumption would be that it must form an exception to the general character of its sister systems. Nothing could be further from the reality. The fundamental principle on which it rests — that the empire is a community of sovereigns, that the diet is a representation of sovereigns, and that the laws are addressed to sovereigns — makes the empire a body without nerve, unable to regulate its own members, insecure against external dangers, and stirred by ceaseless turmoil within.

The history of Germany is a history of wars between the emperor and the princes and states; of wars among the princes and states themselves; of the lawlessness of the strong and the oppression of the weak; of foreign intrusions and foreign intrigues; of demands for men and money that were ignored or only partly complied with; of attempts to enforce them that came to nothing or were attended by slaughter and devastation, swallowing up the innocent with the guilty; in short, of general weakness, confusion, and misery.

In the sixteenth century, the emperor, with one part of the empire on his side, was seen at war with the other princes and states. In one of these conflicts the emperor himself was put to flight and very nearly captured by the elector of Saxony. The late king of Prussia was more than once pitted against his imperial sovereign, and usually proved more than a match for him. Disputes and wars among the members themselves have been so common that the German annals are crowded with the bloody pages describing them. Before the peace of Westphalia, Germany was devastated by a thirty years' war, in which the emperor with one half of the empire stood on one side, and Sweden with the other half on the opposite. Peace was eventually negotiated, and dictated by foreign powers, and its articles, to which foreign powers were parties, became a fundamental part of the Germanic constitution.

If, in some emergency, the nation happens to be more united by the necessity of self-defense, its situation is still deplorable. Military preparations must be preceded by so many tedious discussions, springing from the jealousies, pride, separate views, and clashing claims of sovereign bodies, that before the diet can settle the arrangements the enemy is already in the field, and before the federal troops are ready to take the field, the enemy is going into winter quarters.

The small body of national troops, which has been judged necessary in time of peace, is poorly maintained, badly paid, infected with local prejudices, and supported by irregular and unequal contributions to the treasury.

The impossibility of keeping order and dispensing justice among these sovereign subjects led to the experiment of dividing the empire into nine or ten circles or districts, giving them an internal organization, and charging them with the military execution of the laws against delinquent and stubborn members. This experiment has only served to show more fully the radical defect of the constitution. Each circle is a miniature picture of the deformities of this political monster. They either fail to carry out their commissions, or they do so with all the devastation and slaughter of civil war. Sometimes whole circles are themselves the defaulters, and so they multiply the very mischief they were created to remedy.

We can form some idea of this scheme of military coercion from a sample given by Thuanus. In Donawerth, a free and imperial city in the circle of Suabia, the Abbe de St. Croix had certain immunities reserved to him. While exercising these on some public occasions, he was attacked by the people of the city. As a result, the city was placed under the ban of the empire, and the Duke of Bavaria, though director of another circle, obtained the appointment to enforce it. He soon appeared before the city with a corps of ten thousand troops. Finding it a fit occasion (as he had secretly intended from the beginning) to revive an old claim — on the pretext that his ancestors had allowed the place to be detached from his territory (1) — he took possession of it in his own name, disarmed and punished the inhabitants, and reannexed the city to his domains.

It may be asked, then, what has so long kept this disjointed machine from falling completely to pieces? The answer is obvious. The weakness of most of the members, who are unwilling to expose themselves to the mercy of foreign powers; the weakness of most of the principal members, compared with the formidable powers all around them; the vast weight and influence the emperor draws from his separate hereditary dominions; and the interest he feels in preserving a system to which his family pride is attached, and which makes him the first prince in Europe — these causes prop up a feeble and uncertain Union. Meanwhile the repellent quality natural to sovereignty, which time only strengthens, prevents any reform founded on a proper consolidation. Nor is it to be supposed, even if this obstacle could be overcome, that the neighboring powers would allow a revolution that would give the empire the force and preeminence to which it is entitled. Foreign nations have long considered themselves interested in the changes brought by events in this constitution, and on various occasions have shown their policy of perpetuating its anarchy and weakness.

If more direct examples were needed, Poland, as a government over local sovereigns, might fairly be mentioned. No more striking proof could be given of the calamities flowing from such institutions. Equally unfit for self-government and self-defense, it has long been at the mercy of its powerful neighbors, who have lately had the mercy to relieve it of one third of its people and territory.
The connection among the Swiss cantons hardly amounts to a confederacy, though it is sometimes cited as an instance of the stability of such institutions.
They have no common treasury, no common troops even in war, no common coinage, no common judiciary, nor any other common mark of sovereignty.

They are held together by the peculiarity of their topographical position; by their individual weakness and insignificance; by the fear of powerful neighbors, to one of which they were once subject; by the few sources of contention among a people of such simple and homogeneous manners; by their joint interest in their dependent possessions; by the mutual aid they need for suppressing insurrections and rebellions, an aid expressly stipulated and often required and given; and by the necessity of some regular and permanent provision for settling disputes among the cantons. The arrangement is that the parties at variance shall each choose four judges from the neutral cantons, who, in case of disagreement, choose an umpire. This tribunal, under an oath of impartiality, gives a final ruling that all the cantons are bound to enforce. The competence of this regulation may be measured by a clause in their treaty of 1683 with Victor Amadeus of Savoy, in which he obliges himself to mediate disputes between the cantons and to use force, if necessary, against the stubborn party.

So far as their peculiar situation allows comparison with that of the United States, it confirms the principle being established. Whatever effectiveness the union may have had in ordinary cases, it is clear that the moment a real point of difference came up that could test its strength, it failed. The controversies on religion, which on three occasions kindled violent and bloody contests, may in fact be said to have severed the league. Since then the Protestant and Catholic cantons have had separate diets, where all the most important matters are settled, leaving the general diet little to do besides looking after the common bailages.

That separation had another consequence worth noting. It produced opposite alliances with foreign powers: Berne, at the head of the Protestant association, allied with the United Provinces, and Luzerne, at the head of the Catholic association, with France.
1. Pfeffel, "Nouvel Abreg. Chronol. de l'Hist., etc., d'Allemagne," says the pretext was to indemnify himself for the cost of the expedition.
